blocks.text: Supply side

blocks.html: Dry powder peaked in 2024 at US$634.8bn and edged down to US$618.2bn by mid-2025. On the newly added dry powder as % of NAV measure, the ratio has declined steadily from 66.9% in 2015 to 45.7% in mid-2025, indicating a shift from fundraising-driven growth to deployment of existing capital. The contraction is clearer on the fundraising side: 2025 global private debt fundraising was US$221.2bn across only 206 funds, down 30% and 60% respectively from the 2021 peak (US$318.2bn / 511 funds), with fund count also far below the 2022 record of 568.

blocks.text: Demand side

blocks.html: Private credit remains dominant in LBO financing: on an LTM count basis it financed roughly 80–83% of LBOs as of 1Q26, after peaking near ~90% in early 2023. blocks.text: Non-sponsored private credit

blocks.html: Non-sponsored borrowers — companies with no private equity backing, typically founder- or family-owned — account for roughly 90% of private companies in the US and Europe, yet remain a minority of institutional direct lending: at the last published composition of the KBRA DLD Direct Lending Index, about 600 of its ~2,300 tracked borrowers (~26%) were non-sponsored (Mar-2024), and within our own portfolio Guggenheim PDF IV runs 28% non-sponsored by NAV as of 1Q26.

blocks.html: Pricing has held up better than in the sponsored channel. Sponsor-led, large-cap lending compressed to roughly 400–450bp over base rates through 2025 (50–70bp tighter than at the start of that year), while Cliffwater series show non-sponsor borrower spreads maintaining a premium over directly originated upper-MM loans through 2025. As a 2Q26 market colour point, one middle-market lender described typical non-sponsored terms at ~S+500 with 40–50% LTV, ~4x leverage, roughly 60% equity support and one to two maintenance covenants — materially more lender-protective structures than prevailing sponsored documentation.

blocks.html: The trade-off is a persistently higher default rate. KBRA DLD’s last openly published split put the non-sponsored TTM default rate at 3.5% versus 1.5% for sponsored borrowers (by issuer count, TTM through Mar-2024; non-sponsored names were 23 of 48 defaults from ~26% of index borrowers), and its 2025 forecast kept the gap: 3.75% non-sponsored versus 2.75% sponsored. Current-vintage splits are no longer published openly — KBRA DLD and the Proskauer index both restrict the full sponsored / non-sponsored breakdown to subscribers or clients — so the segment’s spread premium has to be read against this structurally higher default incidence and the absence of a sponsor-equity backstop.

blocks.text: Related news

items: Redemption wave intensified in 2Q26: BCRED requests rose from 7% in Q1 to 10% in Q2; Apollo Debt Solutions from 11% to 17%; Cliffwater CCLFX from 14% to 17%; after HLEND first enforced its 5% cap, the market fell in line. Industry-wide requests are estimated at ~$12bn in 2Q26 and ~$32bn YTD, but gates are working and, in some cases, non-traded funds reported net inflows — liquidity stress is not becoming a solvency problem. An early inflection sign: GCRED's 3Q26 withdrawal requests fell to 4.8% from 8.5% in 2Q — improving, though too soon to call a bottom.

Medallia default and debt-for-control: Lenders led by Blackstone, Apollo and FS KKR took the keys to the software company from Thoma Bravo (a $6.4bn 2021 buyout supported by a $1.8bn recurring-revenue loan), significantly cutting debt and injecting $150m of new capital — the quarter's most watched software default and a live test of recovery assumptions on ARR loans.

Anthropic US$36bn chip-lease financing: Apollo and Blackstone led an investment-grade structured-notes financing for an SPV that buys TPUs and leases them to Anthropic — ~$6bn 'super-senior' A1 (price talk T+100), $25bn first-lien A2 (all-in yield talk 5.50–5.75%) and $4.5bn second-lien B (8.5% fixed), with a Broadcom residual-value backstop. Structured as IG notes, it sits outside LCD's direct lending volume — evidence of private credit pushing into investment-grade / asset-backed territory.

Secondaries and valuation transparency: JPMorgan had traded roughly $2bn of private credit loans by mid-May across 20+ borrowers — more than all prior years combined — at prices from par to 3–10+ points below; Antares completed a $1.7bn continuation vehicle and StepStone closed its second credit-opportunities fund at $1.6bn. In parallel, Apollo will provide daily mark-to-market valuations on all credit assets by 9/30/26 and the US DOL proposed moving private credit closer to 401(k) inclusion — observable prices and regulatory scrutiny of marks are both rising.

Volumes down, sector switch on: The Iran war and the Strait of Hormuz closure stalled M&A: 2Q26 direct lending was just $33bn / 149 deals (vs $74.1bn / 217 in Q1), with no >$2bn direct-lender LBO tracked since early March. Healthcare overtook Technology in new-deal count; >50% of surveyed lenders have cut software exposure (21% significantly, 6% stopped entirely) while 9% added into the dislocation.

items: Software repricing has moved from beta to alpha. Unlike the broad-based 1Q26 repricing, current software-loan weakness is increasingly selective, with much wider dispersion across issuers — investors are underwriting business-model resilience, AI exposure and data moats name by name. Software borrowers must be 'pristine' to get financed, and Vista Credit estimates ~20% of software businesses fall into a 'failure to thrive' bucket. Implication: evaluate our BDC / fund holdings at the single-name level of software composition, not by sector weight alone.

The 2028 refinancing wall did not shrink — it is being pushed out. The near-term BDC maturity wall remains concentrated in 2028–2030 at roughly $80bn per year, and the QoQ snapshot shows the 2031–2033 bucket growing from ~$194bn to ~$207bn while 2026–27 maturities shrink — consistent with amend-and-extend activity deferring rather than resolving the wall (Exhibit 31). Combined with mounting software refinancing pressure and the ~8% default forecast, 2028 remains the operative year of this cycle, corroborating at the industry level the judgement we made on OTF last quarter.

items: Vintage is now the most important stratification variable. The apparently better nonaccrual / PIK metrics of private BDCs largely reflect younger post-2021 vintages, with deeper erosion in pre-2021 books; sub-90 PIK loans are concentrated in IT (8.4%) and healthcare. When diligencing new funds or reviewing incumbent managers, request portfolio metrics split by vintage.

Supply contraction is improving new-deal terms, and the capital base is rotating institutional. Guggenheim observes that non-traded BDCs have cut hold sizes sharply and pulled back from software, and that reduced competition should deliver better pricing, documentation and LTV; its PDF IV's latest six deals carry a weighted average spread of SOFR+546bp, 4.0x first-lien net leverage and a 42% blended LTV — consistent with LCD's recorded +25–50bp spread widening. Meanwhile retail is only ~20% of PC AUM and institutions are re-engaging: Ares closed $8bn+ (~$1bn above target) and Guggenheim PDF IV closed at its $4.5bn hard cap, 50% above the $3.0bn initial target. The current vintage may prove the best-terms deployment window of the cycle.

Junson's three fund holdings show no warning signals this quarter, but marks lag secondary prints. Guggenheim PDF IV held its final close and is deploying normally; PAG BRS Fund III runs a current net IRR of 14.7% / gross 20.8% (and exited Project Veleta in January at a 12% unlevered IRR); HSBC RCF Partnership Fund's watchlist is empty. All three are valued as of 3/31/26 and do not yet fully reflect the 2Q public-market repricing of software and private credit; with PC secondary trading now scaled (JPMorgan ~$2bn; prices par to -10pts), we recommend cross-checking our funds' quarterly marks against available secondary prints.

blocks.text: Cohort health monitor

blocks.html: Beyond our own funds, we track the health of the benchmark cohorts themselves: the QoQ drift of cohort medians and, above all, the width of the interquartile range. Widening dispersion is the early signal that industry stress — software marks, nonaccruals, PIK erosion — is reaching fund-level books. At baseline, the 2023 cohort already shows the widest IRR dispersion of recent vintages (IQR 4.6pp vs 2.1pp for 2021), consistent with the vintage that deployed straight into the 2023–24 wide-spread window now differentiating on credit selection. The 2024 TVPI IQR of just 0.04x reflects a young cohort whose marks have not yet dispersed — watch this widen as the AI/software repricing flows into private marks over coming quarters.

blocks.html: Methodology. Peer universe: PitchBook screen of 333 North America direct lending funds (drawdown structures), exported 13 Aug 2026. Vintage convention (Junson): the vintage of our fund holdings is defined by the year of first investment — PAG BRS III = 2023 (first investments Jul-23), Guggenheim PDF IV = 2024 (May-24), HSBC RCF = 2024 (Feb-24) — consistent with PitchBook's methodology for the peer universe (year of first investment, with final close as fallback), so fund and cohort vintages are like-for-like. Percentile = share of cohort funds with the metric strictly below the fund's value; cohort denominators vary by metric with disclosure coverage. Quarterly process: each quarter the same screen is re-exported, cohort statistics are recomputed on fresh marks, and every metric is diffed against the archived prior-quarter snapshot (this quarter's baseline is archived as CA_snapshot_2026Q3.json). Metric basis: PAG and HSBC figures are fund-level as reported; Guggenheim PDF IV does not disclose fund-level performance, so we use Junson-calculated, investor-level figures as of 2Q26 (net IRR 9.3%, TVPI 1.20x, DPI 0.18x), marked † — investor-level metrics reflect our subscription timing, day-one fee drag and the J-curve of our capital calls and therefore typically sit below fund-level equivalents; †-marked readings are conservative. HSBC RCF's IRR is marked * as ramp-up distorted (2.5% of commitments called; OID-driven early realisations).
